newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka puts off local government polls in north.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka puts off local government polls in north.

text.p: Sri Lankan President Chandrika Kumaratunga has agreed to postpone local government polls scheduled for early 1997 in the north of the country, a leader of the minority Tamils said on Tuesday.

"We said we're not in a position to contest the election physically or politically because we have nothing to offer to the people. She agreed to postpone the election," Douglas Devananda, of the Eelam People's Democratic Party (EPDP), told Reuters.

Devananda said he had three hours of talks with Kumaratunga on Monday along with leaders of the Democratic People's Liberation Front, a former Tamil separatist militia that, like the EPDP, has entered mainstream politics.

Colombo last month announced plans to hold local government elections in Jaffna and three other districts in the north that were recaptured from Tamil Tiger rebels earlier this year. It had called for nominations for the elections this week.

But moderate Tamil political parties in Colombo opposed the plan, saying the north was unsuitable for a peaceful election as vast areas of the region were still under the control of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels.
The government has been pushing Tamil parties to begin political activity in the north as an alternative to LTTE rule.
Devananda said he believed Tamil people in the north were forced to support the LTTE because there was no viable political alternative.

Deputy Defence Minister Anuruddha Ratwatte told parliament last week that Tamil parties should help the government fill the political vacuum in the north and restore civil administration in the region.
The Tamil Tigers have fought the government for 13 years for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in the north and east of the Indian Ocean island.

Most Tamils are Hindus. They make up about 17 percent of Sri Lanka's population of 18 million people, and say they face discrimination in education, employment and language from the Sinhalese Buddhist majority.
